name: Sasak
notes: Sasak (Bahasa Sasak), spoken by ~2-2.7 million on Lombok, West Nusa Tenggara, Indonesia (Austronesian, Malayo-Polynesian; closely related to Balinese and Sumbawa). Four or five dialects with low mutual intelligibility (Kutó-Kuté/Ngenó-Mené, Ngotó-Ngeté, Menó-Mené, Ngenó-Ngené, Meriaq-Meriku); this spec is a dialect-neutral basic-quality description, not tied to one variety. Traditionally written in the Sasak script (aksara Sasaq, an abugida), now largely superseded by a Latin orthography adapted from Indonesian conventions. CONSONANTS: Archangeli, Tanashur & Yip's (2020) JIPA Illustration of the Menó-Mené dialect gives 19 consonant phonemes /p b t d k ɡ ʔ tɕ dʑ m n ɲ ŋ r s h j w l/, matching the mappings here: /p b t d k ɡ/ plosives, /tɕ dʑ/ (⟨c⟩/⟨j⟩) alveo-palatal affricates, /m n ɲ ŋ/ nasals (⟨ny⟩/⟨ng⟩ digraphs), /s h/ fricatives, /r/ rhotic (JIPA: trill word-initially/-finally, tap intervocalically, hence [r]~[ɾ]), /l w j/ approximants (⟨y⟩ for /j/, ⟨j⟩ reserved for the affricate). The glottal stop /ʔ/ occurs only in morpheme-final position (JIPA); the same source's word list shows it is consistently spelled with word-final ⟨q⟩ (e.g. sapaq /sapaʔ/ 'greet', mpaq /mpaʔ/ 'fish', balaq /balaʔ/ 'someone', baliq /baliʔ/ 'puberty'), now modelled as a `positional_graphemes` word-final rule for ⟨q⟩. VOWELS: the JIPA source's Menó-Mené fieldwork finds only SIX vowel phonemes /i e ə a o u/ with no phonemic /ɛ/-/e/ or /ɔ/-/o/ contrast in that dialect; the Wikipedia general-language article instead reports eight vowel qualities /i e ɛ a ə o ɔ u/ across dialects, with the Latin orthography marking the front-vowel contrast diacritically — unmarked ⟨e⟩ = schwa /ə/, ⟨é⟩ = /e/, ⟨è⟩ = /ɛ/, and (per Wikipedia only, not attested in the JIPA fieldwork) ⟨ó⟩ = /o/, ⟨ò⟩ = /ɔ/ for a parallel back-vowel contrast in some dialects/dictionaries — a convention shared with other Nusantara Malayo-Polynesian orthographies (cf. Indonesian ⟨e⟩). Because the /ɔ/ vowel and its ⟨ò⟩ spelling are not attested in the JIPA primary source and the Wikipedia description of it is thin, ⟨ó⟩/⟨ò⟩ remain unmodelled here (a smaller honest inventory). Six diphthongs /ae ai au ia uə oe/ are attested (Wikipedia); word-final /k/ neutralisation is plausible by areal analogy with neighbouring Malayo-Polynesian languages but is not asserted without a citation.
